title: Zardis's loud bass at the Bulls Club and National Park
summary: He moved between bands as work came, never double-booking, and recounts how his unamplified bass carried blocks from the Bulls Club.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: Well I tell you, the way that was, like I told you before, you see I was so much in demand. And they didn't have much fellas to play the bass that after I learned was playing. And this band don't have no job like tonight, or this band got jobs for two, three nights, so maybe, well I'd leave my band, I'd go with that band. You see what I'm talking about? Well this man asked me to join in the band. I said yeah I'll join the band. So I tell this man I can't play them, I'm playing with so and so now. See what I'm talking about? Well all right I'll stay with that band until they don't get no work. Well after they didn't get no work, another band got work and they want me, well I go with that other band. But the way I do that I always keep them in the class all the time. I don't tell them that I want to be with them and be with the other band too. I never did was a man to believe in playing with two bands, you see, because I know I couldn't play with two bands. I had to play with one band, you see. So I was always a straight fellow on that subject, you see. So we got along pretty nice and everything, all the boys, you know, they liked it one or another and what we was doing we liked it. And so that's what makes anybody, I mean anything to take up a few, like what you're doing and you continue on doing it, you know what I mean? You get a kick out of it, that's what I'm talking about. Well that's nice. See right there tonight I played up there? I like that. You see, and I take my bass, I turn my bass, that tone is hitting that wall. See when it hit that tone.
Well I wonder because later you started out facing more of the door and then later you had your bass facing the wall.

That's right, when it hit that wall, that tone's gone, yes Lord. The guy came and asked me, he said, what you got, an amplifier on there? I said no, I don't have no. He said, yeah you got, he said, what makes that bass sound so loud? I said it was just the way I played.
Just the way you played it. As soon as you started out Jaffe came out and said, you really hear the bass tonight?

Yeah. So he looked, he said, man, he said look over there. He said you play as hard. I said I always did, ever since I knew my pitch. I was playing at 8th and Ramport. I was playing at the Bulls Club. Yeah. And you can hear my fiddle from 8th and Ramport to Claiborne and 3rd at the National Park.
You remember the National Park? I've heard about it, yeah.

That's where every time I'd be playing, them guys come up there and say, man, I hear that fiddle way down there. I said, oh good. I said, you're just pulling my leg. He said, no man. He said, really? I hear that fiddle down there. Well all right, if two, three fellas telling you the same thing, you know what I mean? It must be true. Yeah, that's right. I was going with a girl and she lived at Robinson and Thurid. So that night after I knocked off the job I went to her house and she told me, she said, you know, I was up there sitting down looking out the window. You know, I hear that fiddle, this is good. I said, oh you hear somebody else playing. She said, oh no, she said they don't have nothing else on the Monday night. Around here she said, but the Bulls Club. She said that's the only bass she had. So I said, yeah, it must be true then. Because I met a guy who was telling me the same thing, you know what I mean? Yeah, that's strange.
You could hear it that far.
Oh yeah. So I just took it for granted. Sometime I'd be playing at the National Park. And that same old Jack Carey.
